Chivas Regal () is a [blended](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blended_whiskey) [Scotch whisky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotch_whisky) produced by the [Chivas Brothers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chivas_Brothers) subsidiary of [Pernod Ricard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pernod_Ricard) in [Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland).

Chivas Regal was created in 1909 by Chivas Brothers Master Blender Charles Stewart Howard as a 25-year-old luxury whisky.[[1]](#cite_note-1)

1939 saw the debut and continued success of Chivas Regal 12-year-old Blended Scotch in the US, at what was to become a global standard proof value of 75 degrees, i.e., 42.8% ABV.[[2]](#cite_note-auto1-2) (The Americans mark it as 86 proof as they double the ABV to arrive at proof value.) Henceforth, quality, age (generally 12 years), cost (high), popularity (sales) and demography (high-end) would define a "premium" Scotch Whisky.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

In 1997, the Chivas Regal range was expanded with the launch of much older whiskies, such as the Chivas Regal 18 Years Old, and in 2007 the Chivas Regal 25 Years Old.[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-auto62-5) Other expressions followed, like the Chivas Regal Mizunara in 2014, Chivas Regal The Icon in 2015 and the Chivas Regal XV in 2018.

In 2001, [Pernod Ricard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pernod_Ricard) acquired Chivas Brothers.[[6]](#cite_note-6) Its sales grew by 61% between 2002 and 2008.[[7]](#cite_note-7) In global terms, Chivas Regal recorded volume sales of 4.9 million nine-litre cases in 2012 and 2013, but sales decreased to 4.4 million cases in 2015.[[8]](#cite_note-8) It has been the world's fourth-best-selling Scotch whisky since 2016.[[9]](#cite_note-9)[[10]](#cite_note-10) Chivas Regal has been the market-leading Scotch whisky aged 12 years and older in [Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe) and [Asia Pacific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asia-Pacific).[[11]](#cite_note-11)

The vodka is unaged, made using a traditional filtration method developed by P. A. Smirnov. Recipe No. 21 was created by Smirnov's son Vladimir after [escaping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_émigré) Russia during the [October Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/October_Revolution).[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4)

Pyotr Arsenyevitch Smirnov (9 January 1831 – 29 November 1898) founded his vodka distillery in Moscow under the trade name PA Smirnov in 1864, pioneered charcoal filtration in the 1870s, and by 1886 had captured two-thirds of the market in Moscow by virtue of the first use of newspaper advertising while suppressing clerical calls for temperance by generously contributing to the [clergy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clergy). Russian royalty reportedly regarded Smirnov as a favourite. When Pyotr died, his third son Vladimir succeeded him. When the Tsar nationalized the Russian vodka industry in 1904, Vladimir Smirnov was forced to sell his factory and the brand. During the [October Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/October_Revolution) of 1917, the Smirnov family fled the country. In 1920, Vladimir Smirnov established a factory in [Constantinople](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantinople) (present day [Istanbul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul)). Four years later he moved to [Lwów](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lwów) (then in [Second Polish Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Polish_Republic), now [Lviv](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lviv) in Ukraine). He renamed the vodka "Smirnoff". It sold marginally well but not nearly as it had in Russia prior to 1904. Although an additional distillery was founded in Paris in 1925, sales remained far less than that produced in Russia.

In the 1930s, Vladimir met Rudolph Kunett, a Russian who had emigrated in the 1920s to New York City, and had succeeded in business. The Kunett family had been a supplier of grain to Smirnov in Moscow before the Revolution. In 1933, Vladimir sold Kunett the rights to Smirnoff vodka production and sales in North America. However, the business in North America was not as successful as Kunett had hoped. By 1938, Kunett could not afford the sales licenses, and contacted John Martin, president of [Heublein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heublein), a company that specialized in the import and export of liquors and foreign foods. Using the $14,000 that the Heublein company made from a new product that ended up saving them from bankruptcy, Martin bought the rights to Smirnoff in 1939. His board thought he was mad.
